angle: I was a BDR with 5 tools and a spreadsheet. Prioritizing my accounts took 10 hours a month
post_first_line: Prioritizing accounts cost Neema Zarrabian 10 hours monthly.
linkedin_post:
Prioritizing accounts cost Neema Zarrabian 10 hours monthly.

The real damage was hidden in the daily routine behind that number.

Neema started out as a BDR about 5 or 6 years ago. The stack: an intent tool, a sequencing tool, a data tool, Sales Navigator, and a spreadsheet.

Every day started with roughly 2 hours of hunting for data and writing emails. Every day ended with another 2 hours building the call list for the next day.

Then came the monthly reprioritization. Combing through new accounts and ranking them took 10 hours on top of everything else.

Neema was doing all of this from a parents' basement, stitching five different tools together by hand.

That's the part worth noticing. The work wasn't selling. It was moving data between tabs.

When the prep takes more hours than the outreach, the stack is running the rep.

How many hours does your team lose to prep?

Slide 2: Intent tool, sequencing tool, data tool, Sales Navigator
Slide 3: First 2 hours daily: find data, write emails
Slide 4: Last 2 hours daily: build tomorrow's call list
Slide 5: Reprioritizing new accounts took 10 hours every month
Slide 6: The work wasn't selling. It was moving data between tabs.
Slide 7: When prep outweighs outreach, the stack runs the rep.

lesson.title: Your Stack Shouldn't Run Your Rep
takeaways: Five disconnected tools and a spreadsheet turned a BDR's day into manual data work.
Daily prep of roughly 2 hours at each end of the day leaves less time for actual selling.
Monthly account reprioritization at 10 hours is a hidden tax most teams never measure.
lesson.exercise: Track one rep's week and tally the hours spent on finding data, building lists, and prioritizing accounts versus time actually talking to buyers.

angle: It took 6-8 discovery calls to learn my target account was unintentionally breaking the law
post_first_line: Six to eight discovery calls. That's what it took.
linkedin_post:
Six to eight discovery calls. That's what it took.

Neema Zarrabian had one account she was determined to break into, and the answer wasn't anywhere online.

Five years ago, the account was a large school district in the Boston area. Neema lived nearby and wanted to know why they would ever need the product.

The answer only surfaced through discovery. After 6 to 8 calls, Neema learned the district was struggling with a staffing issue tied to its teacher-to-student ratio.

The detail came from the chief of human resources. Nothing online pointed to it.

Looking back, Neema thinks a tool like Unify Chats could probably have surfaced that research, and the news about it, much earlier.

The lesson: when you have a named account list, the real reason an account needs you is often hidden. Finding it takes persistence and the right conversations, plus research that digs deeper than a surface scan.

angle: Outbound has two broken paths: 50 browser tabs or tens of hours building one workflow
linkedin_post:
50 browser tabs open. That's outbound.

There are two ways teams run it today, and both are broken.

Path one is the AE and SDR setup. I see reps working out of Salesforce reports, LinkedIn Sales Nav, and a Chrome extension for pulling contact info. The workflow is extremely manual. Sift through each data point one by one, bouncing across around 50 tabs.

Path two is the other end of the spectrum. GTM engineers have had to build very complicated workflows in a tool like Unify or Clay. You have to connect every data point, decide what happens in every column, and it takes a long time before anything ships.

So you pick your pain. Reps drown in tabs, or engineers drown in workflow builds.

Neither one is a system. One is a pile of manual work, the other is a pile of setup.

Which path does your team live on today?
carousel: Slide 1: Outbound has two paths, and both are broken
Slide 2: Path one: reps working across 50 browser tabs
Slide 3: Salesforce reports, Sales Nav, Chrome extensions, all stitched by hand
Slide 4: Path two: GTM engineers building complex workflows
Slide 5: Every data point and every column needs a decision
Slide 6: One path is manual grind, the other is heavy setup
Slide 7: Which broken path is your team living on?

lesson.title: The two broken paths of outbound
takeaways: The rep-led path relies on Salesforce reports, Sales Nav, and Chrome extensions, and ends up extremely manual.
The GTM engineer path means connecting and deciding on every data point and column in a complicated workflow.
Both paths cost serious time, just in different places.
lesson.exercise: Map how your team does outbound today. Count the tools and tabs a rep touches per account, then note how long your most complex workflow took to build.

angle: Five minutes before a call: how an AE preps with recent news and growth signals instead of org-charting on LinkedIn
post_first_line: Neema Zarrabian preps for calls in five minutes.
linkedin_post:
Neema Zarrabian preps for calls in five minutes.

No org chart. No LinkedIn rabbit hole.

The old way: map out verticals, find the CRO, find the VP of sales, count the BDRs. That takes time most AEs don't have before a call.

Neema's version is one ask: find all the recent news that's relevant, so the call starts with a point of view on where we can help.

For the Vanta call, that surfaced a few things fast. They're launching identity trust platforms, which lines up with how we think about the business. They announced a Series D. They crossed $300 million ARR.

That tells Neema they're growing and investing more in growth. It's exactly the context worth having walking into a call.

Each point comes with an exact timestamp and the sources, so the article is there to read if needed.

It also helps answer a bigger question: are they prioritizing enterprise or SMB?

Prep isn't about knowing everything about an account. It's about knowing what changed recently and what it means for the conversation.

What do you check first before a call?
carousel: Slide 1: Five minutes before a call. No time for LinkedIn org-charting.
Slide 2: Skip mapping verticals, the CRO, the VP of sales, BDR count.
Slide 3: Ask for recent news that's relevant instead.
Slide 4: Vanta example: a new identity trust platform launch.
Slide 5: They announced a Series D and crossed $300 million ARR.
Slide 6: Growth signals tell you where they're investing next.
Slide 7: Timestamps and sources let you verify before you speak.
Slide 8: Enterprise or SMB focus? Recent news helps you answer that.

lesson.title: Five-minute call prep with growth signals
takeaways: Recent news gives you a point of view faster than an org chart does.
Funding and ARR milestones signal where a company is investing in growth.
Sources and timestamps let you check the details before you rely on them.
lesson.exercise: Before your next call, spend five minutes finding the account's latest news, funding, and product launches. Write one sentence on where you can help, based on what changed.

angle: Which AI tool I use for CRM reporting and which for call analysis, and why I split them
post_first_line: Neema Zarrabian split AI tools by job.
linkedin_post:
Neema Zarrabian split AI tools by job.

Win rates, conversion rates, and BDR team metrics used to live in Claude. All of that now lives inside Unify, where Salesforce reporting runs.

Claude still has a job, though. Neema uses it for bulk querying the call recorder to find what was said on each call.

So the split looks like this:

CRM reporting: Unify
Call analysis: Claude

The Unify side goes beyond reporting. Neema also uses it to slice and dice the TAM in different ways, look at accounts the team isn't reaching out to, queue up good accounts for the BDRs, and review AE deals.

One tool doesn't need to do everything. Match each tool to the type of data it handles best.

Which AI tool do you use for call analysis?
carousel: Slide 1: Neema Zarrabian stopped using one AI tool for everything.
Slide 2: Salesforce reporting moved to Unify: win rates, conversion rates, BDR metrics.
Slide 3: Claude now handles bulk queries on the call recorder.
Slide 4: Question to Claude: what was actually said on each call?
Slide 5: Question to Unify: how is the pipeline performing?
Slide 6: Unify also slices the TAM and surfaces accounts nobody is reaching.
Slide 7: It queues up good accounts for BDRs and reviews AE deals.
Slide 8: Split tools by data type, not by habit.

lesson.title: Split your AI tools by the data they handle
takeaways: CRM reporting like win rates, conversion rates, and BDR metrics fits best in a tool connected to your CRM data.
Bulk querying call recordings for what was said is a separate job, and Claude handles it well.
TAM slicing, uncontacted accounts, BDR queues, and AE deal reviews all come from the same account-level view.
lesson.exercise: List your five most common AI tasks this week. Tag each as CRM data or call data, then assign one tool per tag and stick with it for two weeks.

angle: 60-70% open rates, one meeting: why open rate is the wrong number to watch
linkedin_post:
60-70% open rates. One meeting booked.

A question came in from Mary that shows why open rate is the wrong number to watch.

Mary is working about 250 companies with one to three touches each. The opens look fantastic. Only one reply turned into a meeting.

Her question: at what point do you change the messaging, or do you need 7+ touches?

My answer: internally, we focus a lot less on open rates as a performance metric. We focus on reply rates.

Mary's intuition was right. The job is to bring the reply rate up, not to admire the opens.

We're also putting a lot of work into the copywriting skills the agent has access to, so the copy keeps getting better.

But the main lever is simple: make the message as specific as possible.

High opens tell you the subject line and the inbox placement worked. They don't tell you if anyone cared about what you said.

What metric do you hold your outbound to?
carousel: Slide 1: 60-70% open rates. One meeting. Something's off.
Slide 2: About 250 companies, one to three touches, one reply.
Slide 3: Open rate tells you people saw it, not that they cared.
Slide 4: We focus a lot less on open rates internally.
Slide 5: Reply rate is the number to push up.
Slide 6: We keep improving the copywriting skills our agent uses.
Slide 7: The main lever: make the message as specific as possible.
Slide 8: Stop celebrating opens. Start fixing replies.

lesson.title: Why reply rate beats open rate
takeaways: High open rates with almost no replies means the copy isn't landing.
Reply rate is the performance metric to focus on, not open rate.
The best way to improve copy is to make it as specific as possible.
lesson.exercise: Pull your last campaign. Ignore open rate and write down the reply rate. Then rewrite one email so its first line could only be sent to that one company.
